items.abstract:
<jats:p><div>
 We study a specific but important failure mode in financial LLMs: numerical&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 errors in task-specifically fine-tuned small models are statistically&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 structured rather than random (chi-squared = 41.97, p &lt; 0.001), and this&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 structure makes deterministic post-hoc correction more effective than&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 reasoning augmentation in our controlled experiments. Scaling reasoning via&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) —&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 the dominant paradigms for improving LLM numerical accuracy — both degrade&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 performance in this setting (CoT: -9.0pp; RAG: -7.5pp; p &lt; 0.001,&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 McNemar's test).
</div>
<div>
 <br>
</div>
<div>
 We propose a Deterministic Verification Layer (DVL) — a parameter-free,&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 inference-time module that exploits this structured error distribution to&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 improve execution accuracy from 1.0% to 42.61% (95% CI: 39.5–45.7%) on&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 FinQA through document context and QLoRA fine-tuning. DVL logs 63&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 corrections across three rule types with 100% correction precision on the&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 audited subset (44/44 verified correct, zero false positives). All three&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 rules fire on prediction magnitude, question keywords, and document-context&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 unit headers — no ground-truth access at inference. DVL generalizes across&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 architectures (Llama-3-8B: +10.31pp without retraining), across financial&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 benchmarks (TAT-QA zero-shot: +9.47pp and +19.92pp; p &lt; 0.001, McNemar&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 c = 0), and captures 45.8% of gains achievable by full symbolic&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 recomputation (93.13% oracle accuracy) without gold program annotations.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 A cross-domain evaluation on DROP establishes that the structured bias is&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 specific to financial training distributions, not a universal LLM property.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 A mechanistic analysis identifies computational drift as the CoT failure&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 mode: output length increases 17x with zero extraction failures, and a&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 token-level trace shows arithmetic precision degrading at step boundaries.&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 Our system narrows the gap to GPT-3.5 (no CoT) to 5.4pp using a model 25x&nbsp;
</div>
<div>
 smaller, on a single consumer GPU, with deterministic auditable outputs.
</div></jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p><p>We investigate a central question in financial AI deployment: what architectural interventions most reliably reduce numerical hallucination in small language models? Through a controlled ablation of five components on the full FinQA development set (n = 873), we find that deterministic verification is a more reliable pathway to numerical accuracy than reasoning-based prompting in task-specifically fine-tuned 7B models. Our modular pipeline achieves 42.61% execution accuracy (95% CI: 39.5–45.7%), a 42× improvement over the unaugment baseline. A systematic error taxonomy reveals that 73.1% of remaining failures are multi-step reasoning errors, while extraction failures drop to exactly 0% after fine-tuning. Counterintuitively, chain-of-thought prompting (−9.0pp) and cross-document RAG (−7.5pp) degrade performance when applied to a task-specifically fine-tuned 7B model—findings not previously documented in financial NLP. Our deterministic verification layer (a rule-based post-hoc correction module) corrects 54 samples through interpretable, auditable rules without additional training, and maintains its accuracy advantage under simulated real-world noise while fine-tuning alone degrades by up to 10.5pp. We release our model and result publicly.</p></jats:p>
title: Modular Verification Outperforms Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in Small Financial LLMs: A Systematic Ablation Study on Numerical Hallucination Reduction

items.abstract: <jats:p>O uso de Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (LLMs) para prescrição dietética levanta questões de segurança clínica. Este estudo compara a eficácia do ChatGPT, Gemini e DeepSeek na geração de planos hipocalóricos para mulheres brasileiras com sobrepeso. Utilizando prompts one-shot e chain-of-thought, 150 planos alimentares foram gerados e analisados nutricionalmente via TBCA. Os resultados mostram variabilidade energética: o ChatGPT apresentou maior precisão (desvio <0,5%), enquanto os outros modelos superestimaram as calorias. Qualitativamente, todos os modelos falharam: a gordura saturada excedeu os limites em mais de 200% (chegando a 291% no DeepSeek) e foram observadas inadequações sistemáticas de micronutrientes, com o ferro atingindo apenas 55% a 61% das recomendações, além de déficit de cálcio. Conclui-se que a imprecisão qualitativa dos LLMs impede seu uso clínico autônomo, exigindo supervisão profissional.</jats:p>
